Twenty States Receive Grant Funds for Direct Care Workforce Recruitment
5/8/2024
 The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced last week that 20 states have been selected to participate in two separate technical assistance programs that together will help participating states better recruit, train, and retain direct care workers.
The Direct Care Workers (DCW) Strategies Center received applications from 20 states to participate in one of two programs to support them in addressing the workforce shortage in their state. After a thorough assessment, the following six states were selected to participate in the first program:
​
Alaska
Colorado
Delaware
Indiana
New Jersey
New Mexico
Each state will receive up to 250 hours of technical assistance, have a coach, and have access to subject matter experts to support them in addressing their state's unique DCW challenges. The team includes representatives from the state's Medicaid, aging, disability, and workforce development agencies, in addition to other stakeholders.
The remaining fourteen states will be offered an opportunity to participate in a second program offering learning collaboratives focused on sharing best practices, innovative strategies, and proven models for growing the direct care workforce. In addition, each state will receive up to 70 hours of technical assistance on a topic or issue important to the state.

Biden-Harris Administration Partners with States and Releases Data Recommendations to Strengthen the Direct Care Workforce
As part of the Biden-Harris Administration's Care Workers Recognition Month activities and in support of President Biden's Executive Order on Increasing Access to High-Quality Care and Supporting Caregivers, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced today that 20 states have been selected to participate in two separate technical assistance programs that together will help participating states better recruit, train, and retain direct care workers, who provide home and community-based services (HCBS) for older adults and people with disabilities. Both programs are offered through the Administration for Community Living's Direct Care Workforce (DCW) Strategies Center. HHS also announced the first members of the advisory committee that will guide the center's work.
In addition, HHS and the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) released key recommendations for building data infrastructure to support development of policies and initiatives to strengthen the HCBS direct care workforce. As directed by President Biden's care executive order, the recommendations are the culmination of a year-long partnership with DOL that was led by HHS' Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation.
"Investing in care is an investment in the future of America's families, workforce, and economy," said HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra. "Better data infrastructure will ensure that these investments are made wisely, and our partnerships with states will accelerate the development and sharing of effective strategies for expanding the direct care workforce. These announcements reflect the Biden-Harris Administration's commitment to ensuring older adults and people with disabilities can get the care they need to live and thrive in their communities."
"The Biden-Harris Administration is committed to ensuring that workers across the country—including those who work in the crucial and growing care economy for older adults and people with disabilities—have access to good jobs," said Acting Secretary of Labor Julie Su. "Today, the Department of Labor is proud to release a joint report with the Department of Health and Human Services about gaps in data surrounding the home- and community-based workforce. We are also partnering with HHS to uplift the work of the Direct Care Workforce Strategies Center to improve job quality for this essential workforce. In order to better understand this critical sector and to improve job quality for these workers, we need the best possible data. Care workers show up every day to ensure people have the support they need. We need to show up for them to ensure these are quality jobs with family-sustaining wages, safety standards, and benefits."
"Urgent action is needed to address the shortage of direct care professionals – which is threatening to reverse decades of progress in community living," said Alison Barkoff, who leads the Administration for Community Living (ACL). "ACL's Direct Care Workforce Strategies Center was developed in partnership with DOL and agencies across HHS to catalyze that action and to improve recruitment, retention, and development of this critical workforce. The technical assistance announced today will help 20 states improve collaboration across state agencies, direct care professionals, people receiving services, and other stakeholders and accelerate progress toward this goal."
The DCW Strategies Center received applications from 20 states to participate in one of two programs to support them in addressing the workforce shortage in their state. After a rigorous review and scoring process, including interviews with state teams, the following six states were selected to participate in the first program, which offers intensive technical assistance:
Alaska
Colorado
Delaware
Indiana
New Jersey
New Mexico
Each will receive up to 250 hours of individualized technical assistance, have a coach, and have access to subject matter experts to support them in addressing their state's unique DCW challenges. Each team includes representatives from the state's Medicaid, aging, disability, and workforce development agencies, in addition to other stakeholders. Synopses of each state's areas of focus and goals for the program can be found here.
The remaining fourteen states will be offered an opportunity to participate in a second program offering learning collaboratives focused on sharing best practices, innovative strategies, and proven models for growing the direct care workforce. In addition, each participating state will receive up to 70 hours of individual technical assistance on a topic or issue important to the state.
To guide the work of the DCW Strategies Center, twenty-six stakeholders, primarily direct care professionals and people who receive HCBS, were selected to serve as members of the center's inaugural advisory council. A list of the members can be found here.
Making informed policy decisions to expand and strengthen the HCBS workforce can be difficult with the data currently available. Information is often unavailable or incomplete, and much of the data that is available cannot be broken out by state, making it difficult to understand the impact of Medicaid and other policies. That's why President Biden's Executive Order also charged HHS and DOL with identifying opportunities for government and non-government entities to build data infrastructure to inform federal and state policies that strengthen the HCBS workforce, which is disproportionately made up of women, persons of color, and immigrants with little or no formal education beyond high school.
A new issue brief released today by HHS and DOL presents recommendations to improve HCBS workforce data, informed by input from HCBS providers, workers, consumers, and researchers. HHS is taking steps to implement these recommendations, both through the recently finalized Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services rule that will enable greater transparency in rates paid to certain types of HCBS workers, and through the DCW Strategies Center's intensive technical assistance to selected states who have identified data collection, tracking and/or analysis as a key need.
"Implementing these recommendations will build the data infrastructure needed to answer key questions about the HCBS workforce and drive data-informed policy decisions to improve the quality of and access to HCBS for the millions of Americans who are receiving or need these services," said Miranda Lynch-Smith, who is performing the delegable duties of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation.
The report is posted on the DCW Strategies Center website. It will be joined in the coming months by other resources developed through the HHS-DOL partnership.
On Tuesday, May 21, HHS and DOL, in collaboration with the DCW Strategies Center, will host a webinar to share highlights and recommendations from the issue brief. Advance registration  is required.
To learn more, visit the DCW Strategies Center website.
###
Note: All HHS press releases, fact sheets and other news materials are available at https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/index.html.
Like HHS on Facebook , follow HHS on X @HHSgov , and sign up for HHS Email Updates.

State Advancement Lab
States participating in the DCW State Advancement Lab (SAL) receive up to 250 hours of individualized technical assistance from subject matter experts, a designated technical assistance coach, and facilitated collaboration across state agencies to develop state-specific plans to improve and sustain workforce development and retention. The 2025 cohort focuses on three core themes: joining the workforce, well-being at work, and career progression.
Previous Initiatives
2024 Intensive Technical Assistance
Six states were selected to participate in the DCW Strategies Center’s first intensive TA cohort, which concluded in December 2024. Each team included representatives from the state’s Medicaid, aging, disability, and workforce development agencies, in addition to other stakeholders. The state teams completed individualized systems-change TA plans aimed at improving direct care workforce development and retention through reforms in policy, practice, programming, payment, and performance. The intensive technical assistance was designed to build upon states' previous and current workforce efforts, including those undertaken using American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Section 9817 funding.
2024 TA Cohort 

Colorado
The technical assistance provided through the DCW Strategies Center will support Colorado's implementation of key recommendations presented in a research project on workforce compensation initiated in 2022. The state aims to develop an adaptable direct care worker peer mentoring program that can be utilized across various work environments and with different populations. Additionally, Colorado will determine how to help both workers and employers who need access to benefits and services to best navigate them.
About the Team
Led by the Colorado Department of Health Care Policy & Financing, the state’s team also includes the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment and the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment. The state will also engage its Direct Care Workforce Collaborative.

​Congress Re-Launches Assisting Caregivers Today Caucus
7/12/2023
 
​Last week, the bipartisan, bicameral Assisting Caregivers Today (ACT) Caucus was re-launched by Caucus Co-Chairs Sens. Michael Bennet (D-CO) and Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Reps. Jen Kiggans (R-VA) and Debbie Dingell (D-MI). The ACT Caucus will provide education about the challenges family caregivers face and advocate for policies that support them.
“As someone who served as the primary caregiver for parents living with Alzheimer’s disease, I saw firsthand the stress and costs that come with family caregiving,” said WV Sen. Capito. “With the relaunch of the Assisting Caregivers Today Caucus, we are bringing needed attention to the issues caregivers of all backgrounds face. I look forward to working alongside my Senate and House colleagues as we renew our push to find bipartisan ways to lessen the emotional and financial toll for these individuals and families.”
HCAOA is reaching out to the caucus members to learn more.

Newsletter Report HCAOA
The HHCN FUTURE Report How policy, AI and consolidation are reshaping the at-home care market A Home Health Care News Report
December 2025

Insight 1: Embracing innovation, but using it wisely
While the FUTURE conference focuses on forward-looking innovations in the home-based care industry, conversations often returned to the sticky challenges facing home health operators in the present. The Medicare home health 2026 payment rule, for one, was top of mind, as was the rise of Medicare Advantage and staffing shortages. But on stage, speakers’ approach to these hurdles did not involve pausing investments while they strategize for reimbursement cuts. On the contrary, experts emphasized the need for innovation and investment in efficiency-accelerating technologies. It was not just the on-stage experts who were enthused about the latest AI-powered tools. In hallway conversations, provider executives compared notes on their vendors of choice and the technologies that they were interested in. This was most often focused on AI, whether it be ambient listening or documentation tools. Improving the clinician experience, specifically, was top of mind. With so much documentation work necessary for in-home services, and too few workers to deliver these essential services, easing the grunt work lightens the load for each clinician. Interestingly, this added efficiency was rarely referred to as a way to dramatically increase the number of patients each worker could see per day. Instead, this technology was referred to almost exclusively as a way to improve the worker experience and therefore improve retention. David Jackson, CEO of Choice Health at Home, said he hopes efficiency-driving tools could allow clinicians to see perhaps one more patient per day. “You start talking about AI, we definitely need to be talking about how we are enhancing the nurse’s life,” Jackson said. “If it took you three hours to do a start of care and now it’s taking you 55 minutes, you can see more patients. That’s a dance that we’ll play with staffing and … something we have to message correctly as leaders in organizations. ‘We want you to be sitting with your children enjoying dinner at five o’clock, not documenting for the next four hours’.” As hurdles continue to test providers’ abilities to operate with slim margins, cutting-edge technologies are no longer optional. It’s not especially innovative to test the tools that will allow providers to improve clinicians’ experiences and  enhance efficiency. The FUTURE conference revealed that these investments are critical now more than ever, and that to survive current and impending threats, home health companies must evolve their systems and overhaul technologies. 

Insight 2: Through value-based care, home care is no longer on the sidelines
Home care providers have always been a key part of the health care continuum – but may not have always been viewed as such. Non-medical providers are increasingly stepping into roles that demonstrate their value to reducing hospitalizations and improving outcomes, whether it be through the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience (GUIDE) model, or future proofing their organizations for the health care industry’s transition away from fee-for-service dominance. “We are paying very close attention to the shift to value-based care, specifically in non-medical home care,” Crystal Franz, CEO of HomeWell Care Services, said. “Where we used to be on the sidelines of that and the sidelines of the health care continuum as a whole, we now have an opportunity to be a big part of the solution.” Providers are eagerly striding toward this value-based future. Senior Solutions, for example, “wants to be a health care organization. We want to talk about outcomes,” the company’s CEO, Kunu Kaushal, said. Yet, the overlap between value-based structures and home care is in its infancy. The “next hill to climb,” Kaushal said, is establishing the definition of value-based care in personal care. “There will be multiple models, and we all have to test those out,” Kaushal said. “That is how we truly get to the point where someone says, ‘Here is your incentive payment for doing a great job with this certain population within our state.’ Otherwise, we will all continue to fight this war of, can we get another 50 cents per hour?” The future of home care, therefore, involves establishing relationships with payers to demonstrate value and improve reimbursement rates. To do so, providers must also consider social determinants of health, according to Evan Worrell, senior director of operations at Modivcare. 
Caregivers are uniquely qualified to assess and understand social determinants of health, Worrell said, since they are in clients’ homes every day. Considering these factors, like nutrition and rurality, will allow the home care industry to develop a fully-fledged conception of valuebased care, evolve its role in the health care continuum and be rewarded for consistent, quality care. 

Insight 3: Why scale isn’t everything
Broad footprints covering a slew of states can feel like the marker of success for health care businesses. At FUTURE, leaders revealed that breadth should not be the foremost marker of success and should be secondary to density considerations. “Density before scale. That’s so important,” Brian Mills, vice president of acquisitions at Pennant Services, said. “We have three core principles when we’re deciding whether or not to do an acquisition. The first is … do we have the right leadership in place? The second is our own operations that surround [the planned investment], do we have strength where we are able to support and bring on an acquisition? The third is the deal itself, and whether there is quality to be gained and an opportunity to serve in a new community. But those first two points for us are really, really critical.” Growth for growth’s sake can even be detrimental for a business, according to Crystal Franz, CEO of HomeWell Care Services. Processes that work well at a smaller scale can break down if a company attempts to expand without doing so strategically. Considering where to grow is as essential as deciding the strategy to grow. While communities with large facilities for older adults may seem attractive, providers actually should prioritize growing where there is a healthy supply of caregivers, Missy Blankenship, chief operating officer of Arosa, said. Even selecting a location close to public transportation can be crucial to make sure caregivers can get to appointments with clients. Growing for growth’s sake, without a careful plan and focused geographic strategy, cannot be the norm for home-based care providers. In an industry beset by challenges, often chiefly staffing woes, growing successfully does not always mean establishing the broadest possible footprint. Regardless of scale, providers must take a local approach to each community where they operate. Synergy Home Care, for example, is a rapidly growing franchise operation, but it still prioritizes developing presences in each locality it operates in. “Home care is a local business, and the way that you can get to these issues that we’ve been talking about is to embed yourself in your community,” Charlie Young, CEO of Synergy, said.

Newsletter Report HCAOA
Driving Efficiency & Improving Outcomes: Inside the 2026 Tech Landscape for Home-Based Care

Summary of Key Findings
1.) Technology investment is centered on one thing: the client experience. Across the board, home-based care providers are prioritizing client satisfaction as their top tech goal in 2026. From scheduling and intake to documentation, the most in-demand solutions are the ones that can improve day-to-day care delivery and make life easier for both clients and caregivers. 2.) Workforce challenges remain, but the strategy is evolving. While staffing remains the top challenge in home-based care, providers are shifting focus from simply filling roles to creating better work experiences. The data shows a strong push toward improving scheduling, reducing burnout, and increasing compensation as levers for retention, signaling a shift toward longterm workforce sustainability. 3.) AI adoption is still in its early stages, but interest is accelerating. More than 40% of respondents say they’re not currently using AI, but most agree it could drive significant impact. The biggest appetite for AI is in scheduling, back-office automation, and documentation workflows, suggesting that providers are looking to deploy AI in ways that directly address operational pain points, rather than theoretical use cases. 4.) Scheduling is the heartbeat of efficiency and innovation in today’s landscape. Among all of the operational processes highlighted in this survey, scheduling and caregiver matching stood out as one of the highest impact areas for performance improvement. This aligns with both retention efforts and client satisfaction goals, underscoring scheduling as a critical point of convergence between workforce stability and quality care. 5.) Growth plans hinge on partnerships, people, and performance. When it comes to scaling, providers are focused on strengthening referral partnerships, retaining staff, and improving efficiency through technology. These three goals are tightly connected, pointing to a broader strategy of building smarter, more integrated care models that balance capacity with demand. 6.)Effective technology is an organization-wide strategic differentiator. Taken together, the data reveal a shift in mindset around tech adoption in home-based care. Technology is now seen as core to performance across the organization, not just a support function or back office concern. Leaders are investing in tech to improve operations, enable better care, and future-proof their organizations as the pace of change accelerates.

How Technology Is Transforming Care at Home 
Mosai’s Perspective on the Momentum of Home-Based Care Technology

The home-based care industry is standing at a crossroads. On one side, we face growing complexity, with rising patient volumes, staffing constraints, and evolving payment models. On the other, we have unprecedented potential to simplify care delivery through smarter systems and more connected data. This year’s survey results make one thing clear: while AI investment is steadily increasing, interest and appetite have surged far ahead. Providers are exploring how to make these tools work in the real world, not just in theory. And they’re doing it with a healthy dose of skepticism, seeking solutions that support, not replace, the people delivering care. At Mosai, the newly rebranded union of Forcura + Medalogix, we’ve seen firsthand how automation and AI can free up time, reduce noise, and improve clinical confidence when done right. That’s why we’re building tools that don’t just check boxes but actually improve the care experience. It’s our privilege to support this research and to partner with the home-based care leaders shaping what’s next. We’re excited to be part of the journey. Mosai’s Perspective on the Momentum of Home-Based Care Technology Elliott Wood

How Technology Is Transforming Care at Home
83 professionals from organizations that serve the home health and home care industries contributed to the insights in this report, 60% of whom are C-suite executives, VPs, and Directors, each offering their perspective on how companies of all sizes are: 
Summary of Key Findings
Appetite for AI in home-based care has surged in just one year. While current investment levels remain steady, interest in AI has grown dramatically, signaling a sector on the brink of widespread adoption, despite lingering concerns around implementation and real-world use. Providers see the greatest AI potential in streamlining backend workflows, with insurance eligibility, referral data entry, and referral prioritization ranked as top opportunities to boost efficiency. Clinical decision support tools are gaining traction, particularly those that help detect patient risk, guide documentation, and improve staffing allocation. Automated care planning is not yet widely adopted, but more than half of providers expressed strong interest in AI tools that draft or update plans of care. Providers are prioritizing tech that delivers real-time insights during key patient touchpoints like admission, condition changes, and care transitions, where AIgenerated summaries could save time and improve outcomes. While most aren’t using AI to track care plan progress, a majority expressed interest in one-click visibility tools, indicating a growing demand for simpler, smarter tracking solutions. Medicare Advantage preauthorization remains a pain point, with providers calling for real-time status tools and systems that help reduce denial rates. Providers are divided over the burden of hospice eligibility checks, with nearly half saying they are only a minor burden. Yet the majority report at least some burden, suggesting this could be a viable use case for automation. Providers are using a wide range of tools to stay audit-ready, including EHR audit reports, documentation review tools, and manual processes, reflecting a fragmented tech landscape. Referral automation stands out as a clear win, with respondents pointing to faster intake, improved efficiency, and fewer referral errors as major benefits of adopting digital workflows.

Top Targets for AI Deployment in Home-Based Care Respondents see the greatest opportunity for AI in streamlining insurance eligibility (24%) and EHR referral workflows (18%). Referral prioritization and decisioning also stood out, with 16% naming it a top focus area, highlighting growing interest in using AI to support intake efficiency and clinical judgment.

Strong Willingness to Explore Automated Care Planning More than 80% of respondents said they are either already using AI to support care planning or are open to doing so in the future. Only 19% reported no interest, pointing to broad willingness across the market to explore automation in this space.

Strong Interest in Tracking Care Plan Progress A majority of respondents expressed interest in having one-click access to care plan progress throughout the home health episode, with some already using tools that support it.

Key Touchpoints for AI-Generated Summaries Initial admission, changes in condition, and care transitions were cited as the most critical points in the patient journey for AI-generated clinical summaries.

Where AI Decision Support Helps Most Detecting patient risk, supporting documentation and care planning, and predicting staffing needs were the most cited benefits of AI-assisted decision-making.

Eligibility Checks Present a Moderate Time Burden Responses were fairly split on the impact of hospice eligibility checks, with 45% saying they’re not a significant time burden, 43% calling them somewhat significant, and a small share (12%) 6% describing them as a significant strain.

Audit Readiness Tools Vary Widely EHR audit/reporting tools, documentation review systems, and manual tracking are the most common tools used to support audit preparedness

Referral Automation Promises Big Gains Improved efficiency, faster patient intake, and fewer referral errors were seen as the biggest benefits of automating referral acceptance workflows.
